title: Orbital Witness to Offer GenAI Accuracy Insurance in Legal Tech World First
author: Artificial Lawyer

dom.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s emphasis on reliable, accountable adoption by framing safety, reliability and compliance as prerequisites and insurance as only a limited layer of reassurance. It does not, however, provide evidence of substantive verification, task-specific evaluation or improved service outcomes.
qs: Law firms and conveyancing businesses need greater confidence that the AI technology they adopt is safe to use, can be relied upon and is compliant.
To conclude, Boulle stated: ‘We are not saying this is a silver bullet, but we want law firms to feel comfortable.

kp.k: Optional insurance offers redress for generative AI errors
kp.d: Artificial Lawyer reports that Orbital Witness will offer First Title insurance covering errors in its generative AI outputs, sold through the software licence agreement for an additional fee. The article qualifies its claim of a legal-tech world first by reference to the publication's knowledge; this is an announced offering, not evidence of claims paid or demonstrated risk reduction.
qs: First Title will be the insurer and clients will simply pay an additional fee to the tech company to gain this extra level of coverage.

as far as Artificial Lawyer** knows this is the first time a legal tech company has actually offered customers a specific policy guaranteeing them that if its genAI solution gets something wrong, and hence leads to issues for them, they can seek redress via specially designed insurance coverage, which is sold as part of the licence agreement with Orbital Witness.

kp.k: Initial coverage targets AI-assisted residential property documentation
kp.d: The insurance will initially accompany the residential property product, whose reported tasks include extracting information from deeds, comparing reports and flagging issues. Extension to other products, including higher-value commercial transactions, is conditional on how the initial offering goes. The company is also looking to expand into the US and Australia.
qs: the genAI insurance will be offered in conjunction with its residential property product, which helps lawyers with the documentation in real estate transactions such as finding key information in property deeds, comparing information in reports, and flagging any issues.
Depending on how this goes they will look to extend the genAI insurance coverage into other products they offer, such as one for higher value commercial property transactions.
They are also looking to expand into the US and Australia.

kp.k: Auditability underpins error attribution and separate insurance protection
kp.d: Co-founder Edmond Boulle asserts that the product is fully auditable, allowing mistakes to be proven. He describes the optional policy as relatively inexpensive and a fractional addition to software costs, without specifying a price. He expects customers to value coverage that avoids resorting to their own professional indemnity insurance.
qs: ‘Everything we do is fully auditable,’ Boulle explained, hence any mistakes by their product can be proven.
The policy itself will be relatively inexpensive, he added, and a fractional additional cost of using Orbital Witness’s software.

Customers can choose not to have the insurance policy, but Boulle believes that clients will welcome this extra level of security, knowing that if things go wrong they have coverage without having to resort to their own professional indemnity insurance.

kp.k: Client demand helps motivate AI-specific risk coverage
kp.d: Boulle reports that clients have asked about insurance for AI outputs and that the company discussed the issue with several property-sector insurers. The article presents potential business risk reduction for conveyancing providers as a compliance-related rationale, rather than documenting a regulatory requirement or measured reduction in risk.
qs: Boulle noted that they’d been thinking about insurance aspects for some time and had spoken to several insurance companies focused on the property sector.
He added that there is a pull factor here and clients also have asked about the insurance of AI outputs.
having this special insurance for genAI allows providers of residential property work (called conveyancing in the UK) to have potentially a higher level of risk reduction for their business.

kp.k: Fixed fees create incentives for insured AI efficiency
kp.d: Boulle argues that standardised residential property work, often priced at a fixed fee, is well suited to AI. The proposed mechanism is that efficiency increases lawyers' profit margins while dedicated insurance addresses downside risks and demand for safeguards. The article supplies no quantified productivity or profitability findings.
qs: Boulle also noted that in residential property work there is often a fixed fee, work is more standardised, and hence AI tools are a very good fit, as it’s a win-win for the lawyers.
The genAI product plus its own special insurance, addresses both the desire for more efficiency – hence higher profit margins – but also covers downside risks.

kp.k: Insurance is framed as an AI quality signal
kp.d: Artificial Lawyer interprets offering insurance as marketing that signals vendor confidence in output accuracy and differentiates Orbital Witness. Its comparison with a UK quality or safety 'kite mark' is an analogy, not a report of formal certification. First Title CEO Kevin Dick likewise describes the partnership as reassurance for law-firm customers and predicts a benchmark for other providers.
qs: This site added that it’s also a very smart form of marketing, as it shows a very high level of confidence in one’s own product.
In short, having this insurance becomes a type of ‘kite mark’ for the use of genAI in the legal world.
First Title’s innovative insurance policy is the first of its kind and stands to be transformational in the professional services industries, creating a benchmark for other AI providers to aspire to.

kp.k: Lawyer-focused regulation complicates direct oversight of AI software
kp.d: The publication characterises the general position of legal regulators in England and Wales as concern about generative AI coupled with a remit focused on lawyers rather than software. It says this makes detailed regulation of AI product use difficult and acknowledges that the position may change. No particular regulator, rule or formal decision is identified.
qs: in England & Wales the general message from legal regulators here is that while genAI concerns them, ultimately they handle the regulation of lawyers, not software, so it’s not easy for them to get into the details of what you can and cannot do with an AI product.
That said, this position may change – but more on that another time.

kp.k: Wider adoption is predicted, not demonstrated
kp.d: Boulle explicitly qualifies insurance as not being a complete solution, while predicting that more legal-sector providers will adopt it. Artificial Lawyer leaves open whether this will remain a one-off or spread across legal technology companies.
qs: We are not saying this is a silver bullet, but we want law firms to feel comfortable. We believe we are the first to do this in the legal sector, but we will see more of this.
Will Orbital Witness’s genAI insurance be a one-off, or will many other legal tech companies follow their example?

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Artificial Lawyer reports that Orbital Witness will offer optional insurance covering harmful errors in its generative AI outputs, initially for residential property work.
pts.d: The announced arrangement makes specially designed insurance available through the software licence for an additional fee, with First Title as insurer. The residential product assists lawyers by extracting information from deeds, comparing reports and flagging issues. Artificial Lawyer qualifies its description of the offering as a legal-tech world first by reference to its own knowledge. The announcement concerns insurance redress for errors, not a claim that the software cannot err.

pts.k: Edmond Boulle presents AI plus dedicated insurance as a way to improve conveyancing efficiency and margins while reassuring firms about downside risks.
pts.d: In the article's account of Boulle's argument, standardised residential property work and frequent fixed fees make AI particularly suitable: efficiency gains can increase lawyers' profit margins. Boulle expects customers to welcome separate coverage rather than having to resort to their own professional indemnity insurance. He describes the additional cost as fractional and says the product is fully auditable, allowing mistakes to be demonstrated.

pts.k: Artificial Lawyer interprets the insurance as a market differentiator and quality signal; Boulle predicts further adoption of this approach in the legal sector.
pts.d: The author argues that offering insurance signals confidence in output accuracy and can function as a metaphorical 'kite mark' for legal generative AI; the article does not describe an actual certification award. Boulle predicts more such offerings, while the author leaves open whether competitors will follow. Separately, First Title CEO Kevin Dick claims AI is speeding up and reducing the cost of real estate transactions and describes the partnership as potentially transformational for professional services.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on an announced commercial arrangement, company and insurer statements, and the author's interpretation rather than measured results.
pts.d: The concrete basis is the described Orbital Witness–First Title insurance offering. Boulle supplies company testimony about auditability, insurer discussions and customer requests for coverage. His account of standardised, fixed-fee conveyancing supports the efficiency-and-margin argument. Dick provides the insurer's endorsement. The source presents no quantitative accuracy tests, transaction-time or cost comparisons, premium amounts, claims-payment experience, or detailed policy terms. First-in-market status is qualified by the publication's knowledge and Boulle's belief; broader diffusion and transformational effects are predictions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The June 2024 article announces a prospective residential-property offering; product expansion and wider adoption remain conditional or undated.
pts.d: As of 25 June 2024, the source says the insurance 'will' be offered, without specifying a launch date. Customers must opt in and pay extra. Redress is described in relation to incorrect outputs that cause issues, without specifying coverage limits or exclusions. Expansion to other products, including higher-value commercial property work, depends on the initial experience. US and Australian expansion is an intention, not a completed rollout or a definite commitment to insurance availability in those markets. Boulle's prediction of more such offerings and Dick's transformational forecast have no deadline. The efficiency argument is especially tied to standardised, fixed-fee work.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate affected parties are residential conveyancing lawyers and firms buying Orbital Witness software, alongside the vendor and insurer; other property segments and AI providers are prospective beneficiaries or followers.
pts.d: Law firms and conveyancing businesses are offered document-processing assistance, potential efficiency and margin gains, and an optional route to insurance redress distinct from their own professional indemnity coverage. Orbital Witness is positioned as gaining market differentiation, while First Title supplies the insurance. Commercial-property practitioners could receive coverage if the offering expands. Other legal-tech and AI vendors are identified as possible imitators. Dick extends the predicted significance to professional services generally. The source does not establish direct access-to-justice effects or specify how savings would be passed to property clients.
